html:
1

About a Quarter of Math Questions Have No Answer Choices

These are called Student Produced Responses (AKA grid-ins). You type in the answer yourself. A right answer typed the wrong way does not earn the point, so the format is worth two minutes of your life right now.

Fraction or decimal

Either one counts.
1/2, .5 and 0.5 are all correct.

Long decimals

If it does not fit, fill every space. For two thirds, .6666, .6667, 0.666 or 0.667 count. .67 does not.

Mixed numbers

A whole number plus a fraction, like 3 and one half (written 3½), is read as 31/2. Type 7/2 or 3.5.

No symbols

No percent % signs, dollar $ signs or commas. If the answer is 25 percent, type 25.

Negatives

Same rules apply. Just be sure to type the minus sign first.

More than one answer

Enter just one of them. Never a list like “0.5 or ½”. Just pick one!

Use the Answer Preview. Bluebook shows a preview of how it read your entry. Glance at it every time; it catches a stray character or a fraction typed as a decimal before you submit. Answers can be at most 5 characters if positive, 6 if negative (the minus sign counts).
2

Sprint: Would It Earn the Point?

The correct answer is on the left. A student typed the entry on the right. Tap Accepted or Not accepted, or press A / N. Under three seconds an item is test speed.

Every item is decided by one of the six rules above.

3

Practice: Type It In

Now the real thing. Each answer is given in words. Type it the way you would in Bluebook, watch the preview, and press Check. The checker follows College Board’s rules exactly: digits, one decimal point or one fraction bar, a minus sign first if needed, five characters (six with a minus), and nothing else.

4

Do They Provide Any Formulas?

Yes. Bluebook has a reference sheet you can open and close on any Math question. It covers geometry and basic trig. It does not cover algebra, which is most of the test, so the quadratic formula, slope, exponent rules, and the like must be memorized. Here is what the popup contains:

Circle

$$A = \pi r^{2} \qquad C = 2\pi r$$

Rectangle & Triangle

$$A = \ell w \qquad A = \tfrac{1}{2}bh$$

Right Triangle

$$c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$$

Pythagorean theorem

Special Right Triangles

$$30\text{–}60\text{–}90:\ x,\ x\sqrt{3},\ 2x$$ $$45\text{–}45\text{–}90:\ s,\ s,\ s\sqrt{2}$$

Box & Cylinder

$$V = \ell w h \qquad V = \pi r^{2} h$$

Sphere

$$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}$$

Cone & Pyramid

$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^{2} h \qquad V = \tfrac{1}{3}\ell w h$$

Angle Facts

$$360^{\circ} = 2\pi \text{ radians in a circle}$$ $$\text{Triangle angles sum to } 180^{\circ}$$

Memorize these. They are NOT on the sheet: quadratic formula $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a}$, vertex $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}$, slope $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$, distance $\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$, midpoint $\left(\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right)$, exponential growth $A = P(1 + r)^{t}$, circle $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$.

See the official sheet. Khan Academy posts the exact reference sheet Bluebook shows you: Digital SAT Math Official Formula Reference Sheet.
